name: Vanta Ordnance Phalanx VO-8 'Centurion'
description:
A dual-purpose support weapon that alternates between kinetic suppression fire and a projected kinetic barrier. The Phalanx uses a single electromagnetic accelerator that can either fire 5mm tungsten rounds at 600 RPM or redirect its magnetic field to generate a localized shield that deflects incoming small-arms fire.

Vanta Ordnance designed the Centurion for small-unit operations where a team cannot carry both a support weapon and a shield generator. The VO-8 allows a single operator to switch between offensive and defensive roles in under half a second, providing suppressive fire during movement and shield coverage during pauses.

The trade-off is that the weapon cannot fire and shield simultaneously — the electromagnetic system does one or the other. Operators describe using the Centurion as a rhythm: fire, shield, advance, fire, shield, advance. Skilled operators develop an intuitive sense for when to switch modes, creating a pulsing offensive/defensive cadence that is difficult for opponents to exploit.
legality: Licensed — military and corporate tactical units
specifications: caliber: 5mm tungsten (fire mode) effective_range: 50-600 meters (fire mode), 3-meter radius (shield mode) rate_of_fire: 600 rounds per minute (fire mode) capacity: 300-round magazine weight: 13.8 kg power_source: Dual-mode capacitor bank, shared between fire and shield functions
tactical_use: The Centurion is deployed in small-unit assaults where the team needs both fire support and mobile cover. The weapon's operator becomes the tactical fulcrum of the team — suppressing threats during movement phases and providing cover during consolidation phases. In corridor and room-clearing operations, the Phalanx operator typically leads, projecting a shield for the team's approach and switching to fire mode once the entry point is reached.
cultural_context: Vanta Ordnance's dual-mode philosophy has attracted operators who view themselves as protectors rather than pure combatants. Centurion operators often come from defensive security backgrounds and take pride in the weapon's shield capability as much as its lethality. In the contractor community, Phalanx operators are respected for their tactical judgment — the decision of when to fire and when to shield determines whether their team lives or dies.
story_hooks: A Centurion operator discovered that the shield mode generates a resonance frequency that disrupts nearby electronic systems — an unintended EMP side effect that Vanta is trying to keep quiet before it becomes a selling point.

Two Phalanx operators faced each other in a corridor — one shielding, one firing, then switching. The engagement lasted eleven minutes before both ran out of power simultaneously. Neither side is willing to discuss what happened next.

physical_description.visual_profile: A imposing, angular support weapon with a pronounced forward-swept profile. The body tapers from a bulbous receiver housing down to a narrower barrel assembly, giving it an almost predatory silhouette. Electromagnetic field coils wrap visibly around the barrel in a helical pattern. The overall impression is military-industrial and deliberately intimidating — a weapon designed to be seen and respected.
physical_description.dimensions: 127 cm length overall, 8 cm receiver width, 6 cm height at coil assembly. 61 cm barrel length with integrated field resonator.
physical_description.weight_description: Hefty and purposeful at 13.8 kg. Balanced slightly forward toward the barrel, requiring a strong stance and deliberate control. Feels anchored to the shooter rather than quick-handling.
physical_description.primary_material: Reinforced composite polymer frame with integrated steel load-bearing skeleton. Barrel assembly is heat-treated steel with chromium carbide coating. Electromagnetic coils are wrapped copper wound around ferrite cores.
physical_description.finish: Matte gunmetal polymer with brushed steel accents on the barrel and receiver housing. Heavy use in field conditions shows worn polymer edges and burnished spots where gloved hands grip repeatedly. Some units display light scorching from electromagnetic field stress.
physical_description.color_scheme: Charcoal gray primary with gunmetal steel secondary. Accent lines in deep blue running along the electromagnetic coil housing, marking the field generation zones. Optional corporate unit markings in reflective white or unit colors.
physical_description.grip_texture: Rubberized overmold with aggressive diamond-pattern knurling. The forestock features a wraparound palm-swell designed for sustained gripping during both fire and shield phases. Textured polymer charging handle with serrated edges.
distinctive_features: Helical electromagnetic coil assembly running the length of the barrel — three primary coil rings with visible copper windings
Dual-mode indicator array: small LED cluster (red for fire mode, blue for shield mode) mounted on the upper receiver
Heat dissipation fins along the receiver housing — necessary for rapid mode switching without thermal buildup
Integral top-mounted field strength gauge with analog needle, glowing faintly in low light
Magazine well recessed slightly, accepting 300-round drum magazines with audible seating click
Rear dampening system with visible pneumatic buffers to manage recoil during sustained 600 RPM fire
Small maintenance access panels on both sides, marked with caution striping
Forward bipod assembly that deploys for stabilized fire or shield projection — folds flush when retracted
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: VANTA ORDNANCE stamped in bold sans-serif font across the upper receiver. Serial number and date code engraved on a discrete steel plate inset into the left side of the frame. Tier 4+ licensing mark stamped near the magazine well. Small Φ symbol indicating cost-of-manufacture certification beneath the field gauge.
physical_description.condition_typical: Field-worn and well-maintained. Scuffing on the polymer from gloved handling and tactical gear contact. The barrel shows light oxidation patina from electromagnetic stress. Most operators keep the coil assembly clean of debris, as contamination affects field projection. A few cosmetic dings and scratches are expected; structural damage is rare given the robust composite design. Well-maintained units show clear indicator lights and responsive mode-switching. Neglected examples display sluggish response times and dimmer status displays.
